Adding frequency data from another affected user — this is not a rare edge case.

**Environment**
- OpenCode: 1.18.21
- OS: Windows 11 (native, not WSL)
- Model: `opencode/x-preview-f-free` via the opencode gateway
- Hit in both `primary` and `compaction` agent modes

**Log evidence (`~/.local/share/opencode/log/opencode.log`)** — **607 stream errors in ~6 weeks**, all matching this pattern:

```
level=ERROR message="stream error" providerID=opencode modelID=x-preview-f-free mode=primary error.error="AI_APICallError: Service Unavailable"
```

Daily breakdown:

| Date | Errors | Date | Errors |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jul 26 | 93 | Aug 14 | 166 |
| Aug 12 | 45 | Aug 16 | 109 |

Spikes cluster on specific days, consistent with server-side capacity issues on the shared free gateway rather than client-side faults.

**User-visible behavior:** matches this issue exactly — the turn ends silently mid-"thinking", no error is rendered in the TUI, and the session appears idle. The user has no way to distinguish "model finished" from "stream died" without manually checking logs.

**Expected:** failed streams should be retried with backoff and/or surfaced as an explicit error in the TUI, per the OP in this issue.

Happy to provide full logs if useful.

Under heavy workload in TUI, Opencode runs a Git snapshot before and after every
agent turn. With 10 parents and 80 subagents, these snapshots run concurrently
across repositories without a global limit.
In 322 seconds, this path started 7,005 Git processes, representing 78.7% of
all observed process starts. During the same period, median `/api/health`
latency increased from 2.9 ms to 318 ms and the TUI became approximately twice
as slow.
The CodeNomad test reproduced the same Git/ripgrep fan-out. The concrete
bottleneck is therefore the per-turn Git snapshot subprocess churn in the
shared daemon.

Confirmed still reproducible on **v1.18.19** (current release), but I found a **working local workaround** — no code change needed.

### Workaround (tested working)

Pin `small_model` to a model that works. This is my config — I tested it in a fresh session and the title agent auto-generates titles correctly.

Add `small_model` to your global opencode config at **`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`** (i.e. the `opencode.json` under the `.config/opencode/` folder in your home directory):

```json
"small_model": "ollama-cloud/deepseek-v4-flash:0731"
```

`Provider.getSmallModel` checks `cfg.small_model` first (provider.ts:1917) and returns that model regardless of the session's provider, so even with the `opencode` provider (e.g. `big-pickle`, which otherwise resolves to `gpt-5.4-nano` and fails) the title agent now works.

> Note: after editing, open a **new** session to test — existing sessions keep their already-failed `New session - <timestamp>` title.

### For others who don't use ollama-cloud

If you don't use ollama-cloud, `opencode/big-pickle` is a free model on the `opencode` provider you can use instead:

```json
"small_model": "opencode/big-pickle"
```

> Caveat: `big-pickle` sits on the **same `opencode` provider** that `smallOptions()` in `src/provider/transform.ts` still lacks a case for, so it may not be bulletproof for everyone. If you hit the free-tier quota or it still fails, just point `small_model` at any other model/provider you prefer.

### Alternative: a local lm-studio model

If you run lm-studio locally, you can point `small_model` at a small local model (e.g. `lm-studio/nvidia-nemotron-3-nano-4b`). It's free, private, and not subject to cloud quotas:

```json
"small_model": "lm-studio/nvidia-nemotron-3-nano-4b"
```

A small/fast local model is ideal for title generation, which only needs a short summary of the first message. Just make sure the local model is loaded in lm-studio when you start an opencode session.

### Status of the actual fix

Still not fixed in source — `smallOptions()` has no `opencode` branch (only `openai`, `openrouter`/`llmgateway`, `venice`), while the normal `options()` does set `promptCacheKey`/`include`/`reasoningSummary` for `providerID.startsWith("opencode")`. Both prior fix PRs (#31760, #31092) closed without merging. Would be great to re-land one of them.

Requesting this PR be reopened. It was auto-closed by the cleanup bot (created >1 month ago, <2 positive reactions), but it fixes a real, still-active bug — it should not have been swept up.

**The bug is still present in the latest release (v1.18.19):** auto session title generation silently fails for `opencode` (Zen) provider models, because `smallOptions()` in `src/provider/transform.ts` still has no `opencode` branch (it only handles `openai`, `openrouter`/`llmgateway`, and `venice`). Issue #30662 is open and multiple users are affected.

This PR is the proper fix: it adds the missing `opencode` handling to `smallOptions()` (the same `promptCacheKey`/`include`/`reasoningSummary` that `options()` already sets), plus a useful warning when a configured `small_model` isn't found. Author verified: `bun typecheck` passes, provider tests 88/88, transform tests 250/250 (+2 new for opencode).

A config workaround exists (`"small_model": "<working-model>"`), but it shouldn't be required — users on the `opencode` provider hit silent title failure by default. Could a maintainer review and reopen this so it can be merged?

Three things I can add, one of which is a second bug on the **local** side that is the mirror image of the one reported here — it charges *too much*, in a band nobody has looked at yet.

### 1. The deprecated 200k field silently overrides the real threshold

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/3a31c4ea801915c0b050df4b3842997ea62b6e93/packages/opencode/src/session/session.ts#L380-L386

The `??` fires whenever the tier filter comes back **empty** — and the filter is empty precisely when the request is *below* the real threshold. So control then falls to `experimentalOver200K && contextTokens > 200_000`, which is a different, hardcoded number.

That matters for any model that carries both fields, and models.dev gives `gpt-5.6` and `gpt-5.6-luna` a `tiers` entry at 272 000 *and* a `context_over_200k` block. Running that expression against the real models.dev payload for `gpt-5.6-luna`:

| context tokens | costInfo.input | documented |
|---|---|---|
| 199 000 | $0.20/M | $0.20/M |
| 200 001 | $0.40/M | $0.20/M ❌ |
| 250 000 | $0.40/M | $0.20/M ❌ |
| 271 999 | $0.40/M | $0.20/M ❌ |
| 272 001 | $0.40/M | $0.40/M |

Every Luna request between 200 001 and 272 000 tokens is estimated at **2× the documented rate**, and the same holds for `gpt-5.6` ($5 → $10/M). This is the exact band @Zaczero measured 94 requests sitting in on Zen — so in that band the local estimate and Zen are wrong *in the same direction*, for two unrelated reasons.

The fix is not to touch the constant but to stop reaching the fallback at all when `tiers` is present: fall back only when `cost.tiers` is absent or empty, not when it is present-but-unmatched.

### 2. The threshold is 200k for Grok and 272k for the GPT-5.6 family — not one number

> the one-line fix is to stop using `200_000` and read `cost.tiers[0].tier.size` (272 000 for Luna / Grok / the GPT-5.6 family)

The first half is right; the parenthetical is a trap. models.dev has `xai/grok-4.6` and `xai/grok-4.5` at `tier.size: 200000`, and [xAI's own models page](https://docs.x.ai/docs/models) splits every Grok row at `< 200k` / `≥ 200k prompt tokens`. 272 000 is the OpenAI number. @dpclark4's report is a **grok-4.6** session, so it is a 200k model, and @Zaczero's 302-request burst is Luna, a 272k model — two different thresholds in the same thread, which is the strongest argument there is for reading the field rather than substituting a new constant for the old one.

### 3. `>` versus `>=` at the threshold is vendor-specific, and the schema cannot express it

Line 382 uses strictly-greater for every provider. Vendors do not agree about the token *at* the line, and it is not a rounding question — they say opposite things in prose:

- **xAI** — "requests whose prompt **reaches** the listed token threshold are billed at the higher rate for all tokens in the request" ([docs.x.ai/docs/models](https://docs.x.ai/docs/models), read 2026-08-22). Exactly 200 000 → **high** tier. `>` undercharges here.
- **Google** — "$2.00, prompts **<= 200k** tokens $4.00, prompts **> 200k** tokens" ([Gemini API pricing](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing), read 2026-08-22). Exactly 200 000 → **low** tier. `>` is correct here.
- **OpenAI** — only a row label, `gpt-5.5 (<272K context length)`, never stated in prose ([pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing)). Inclusive by the label, but inferred rather than quoted.

Same number, opposite answer, at the two vendors that share 200k. One token, so it is worth far less than #1 — but there is no field in models.dev's `tier` object to record it, so no consumer of that data can be right for both vendors no matter what operator it picks. I've written the boundary semantics up per vendor with the quotes here: https://xyzs996.github.io/llm-api-pricing/prices.html#same-number-opposite-answer — and filed the same question upstream at pydantic/genai-prices#587, which has the identical `>`-for-everyone comparison.

Happy to send a PR for #1 if that shape of fix is

Thanks for keeping #2242 open — adding a follow-up since my comments on 2026-06-05.

Verified today (GUI/Desktop focus, since #2242 is about Desktop too):
* **Codex Desktop (benchmark)**: Proper native Windows sandbox on Desktop and CLI — elevated (`CodexSandboxOffline`/`Online` users + `WRITE_RESTRICTED` + synthetic SID + firewall) / unelevated fallback — https://openai.com/index/building-codex-windows-sandbox/ — gives the UX I like: auto-accept inside workspace, ask when trying to write outside or need network, OS-enforced.
* **Claude Code (Anthropic, correcting transcription)**: Docs explicit `Native Windows is not supported. Sandboxing requires WSL2` https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing — even via its VS Code extension / Desktop surfaces, no native Windows OS sandbox (feature request #46740 closed stale).
* **OpenCode Desktop**: Still `experimental.sandbox` macOS-only Seatbelt (#21538). On native Windows (CLI and Desktop) only `permission` (`allow`/`ask`/`deny`) with no OS enforcement — and Desktop's `Auto-accept permissions` toggle is currently disconnected from runtime (#38154 / #38289).
* **Command Code Desktop**: No native Windows OS sandbox either, but permission UX is ahead of OpenCode (`default` / `auto-accept` / `plan` / `bypass` + `Shift+Tab`, `deny` > `ask` > `allow`) — so it gets the auto-accept inside, ask outside flow on top of permissions, just without kernel enforcement.
* **Cursor Desktop**: Included for completeness as the other major GUI — sandbox story is similar to Claude/OpenCode (no native Windows kernel sandbox, relies on permission prompts).
CLI-only harnesses like DeepSeek Harness (Windows ACL `partial`), hermes or pi have experimental Windows backends but no Desktop GUI, so leaving them out here for scope — happy to add if useful.

For OpenCode Desktop this still leaves native Windows users without any OS-enforced boundary, unlike Codex. Even a first step — automatic ask on outside-write / new domain instead of only manual `permission` rules — would already help a lot before full kernel enforcement.

Is there an ETA or plan to bring a Codex-style restricted-token approach to OpenCode on Windows Desktop? Happy to help test a Windows preview or open a focused Windows-Desktop sandbox request if preferred.

While writing it I checked the whole models.dev catalog rather than just Luna, and the case is stronger than I put it above. `context_over_200k` is not a second, cheaper threshold — it is the lowest context tier under an older name:

- **361** models carry both `tiers` and `context_over_200k`
- in **all 361**, its prices equal the lowest context tier's exactly
- **0** models carry it without `tiers`

So the fallback is only ever reached below the real threshold, where the base price is the right answer. **252** tier entries sit at a threshold other than 200k (137 at 272k, 56 at 256k, 31 at 128k, 20 at 32k, 6 at 512k, 2 at 262144), and each has the same overcharged band.

One correction to my own comment: this does not touch @dpclark4's grok-4.6 case, since Grok's real threshold *is* 200k, so the fallback and the tier agree there. The $3.37 vs $3.71 gap is still the Zen side @Zaczero traced.

I captured a redacted OpenCode session trace that reproduces the model-side behavior described here. The session used GPT-5.6 Sol.

The original JSON export parsed successfully. Archive fingerprint: SHA-256 `705aedb6911958debf5125eac499f31fc90a68ce9dc4235685e9637ba0a7fa6e` (164,608 bytes). I am intentionally not attaching the full export because it contains encrypted reasoning payloads, task prompts/tool data, unrelated conversation content, and local/session metadata.

Relevant trace (UTC):

1. At `2026-08-22T18:47:24.146Z`, I explicitly asked the assistant to mark two current tasks as in progress (`messages[22].parts[0]`).

2. At `2026-08-22T18:47:24.225Z`, it refused before calling the tool (`messages[23].parts[5]`):

   > 不能把当前清单中的两个任务同时标为 `in_progress`
   >
   > “I can't mark two tasks in the current list as `in_progress` at the same time.”

   It attributed the refusal to its effective instruction requiring a single active Todo.

3. No `todowrite` call was emitted after that request (searched all remaining messages, `messages[22..27]`). This was therefore not a backend/API rejection of a multi-active update: the model declined before invoking the tool.

There is also useful control evidence in the same trace. Earlier, the assistant emitted three `background: true` task-launch calls in one response, with launch timestamps only 70 ms apart (`messages[14].parts[1..3]`). Concurrent background dispatch was available while the Todo representation remained constrained to one `in_progress` item.

The narrow conclusion from this trace is:

- the single-`in_progress` instruction can make the model refuse to represent multiple active tasks;
- this couples Todo representation to scheduling and pressures the model toward a serial plan; and
- it is not evidence of a backend one-task concurrency limit.

The trace does not by itself contain a complete sequence of otherwise-parallel work being executed serially. It directly demonstrates the prompt-following failure mode behind this issue: the model treats the single-active wording as a binding platform constraint before the TodoWrite handler is called.

### Bug Description
I am experiencing a severe performance/freeze issue with the OpenCode Agent status lifecycle. 

After starting a session or agent workflow, the agent status indicator shows **Active** for approximately ~1 minute before automatically shifting back to **Inactive** (indicated by a red status badge). Immediately following this state transition, the entire application interface freezes, stops responding to user interactions, and remains hung indefinitely.

The only way to recover from this state is to forcefully terminate and restart the application.

---

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Open **OpenCode Desktop**.
2. Select and initialize the target **Agent** for a session/task.
3. Observe the status indicator in the agent panel (it turns active green/blue).
4. Leave the agent running/processing for ~60 seconds.
5. **Observed Behavior:** 
   - Status badge toggles to **Inactive (Red)**.
   - Main thread UI locks up completely (no click, scroll, or input response).
   - Require application restart to unfreeze.

---

### Expected Behavior
- The agent should remain in the `Active` state until the process/task is completed or explicitly paused.
- If the agent disconnects or hits an error, the UI should handle the fallback gracefully (e.g., displaying a non-blocking error toast) without locking or crashing the main application thread.

---

### Environment & Context

The boundary case in the new test is pinned to the wrong side for xAI specifically, and it's worth catching now because the test will freeze it.

```ts
expect(estimate(200_000)).toBe(0.4)   // 200,000 × $2/M — base rate
```

xAI documents the opposite:

> requests whose prompt **reaches** the listed token threshold are billed at the higher rate for all tokens in the request

— <https://docs.x.ai/docs/models> (read 2026-08-22; the note sits under the text pricing table, and the tables give 200k prompt tokens as the cutoff — e.g. grok-4.6 going $2.00 → $4.00 per million input). "Reaches" is `>=`, so a prompt of exactly 200,000 is billed at the long-context rate. That line should be `toBe(0.8)`.

The cause isn't in this PR — `session.ts:384` already reads `contextTokens > 200_000`, and the generic ladder above it reads `contextTokens > item.tier.size`. This PR just wires the config through and adds the first test that lands exactly on the line, so it's the point where the off-by-one gets locked in.

**The fix is not a global `>` → `>=`.** Vendors genuinely disagree about which side the threshold token falls on, so the comparison can't be a constant in the ladder code:

| vendor | documented wording | prompt exactly at threshold |
|---|---|---|
| **xAI** | "requests whose prompt **reaches** the listed token threshold are billed at the higher rate for all tokens in the request" | **long-context** |
| Google (Gemini 2.5 Pro) | `$1.25, prompts <= 200k tokens` / `$2.50, prompts > 200k tokens` | standard |
| OpenAI (gpt-5.4/5.5) | "prompts with **>272K** input tokens are priced at 2x input and 1.5x output for the full session" | standard |
| MiniMax (M3) | `≤ 512k input tokens` / `> 512k input tokens` | standard |

All read 2026-08-22: <https://docs.x.ai/docs/models>, <https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/pricing>, <https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.4>, <https://platform.minimax.io/docs/guides/pricing-paygo>.

So `contextTokens > item.tier.size` is correct for three of the four and wrong for the one this PR is actually about. The narrow fix is `>=` for the `experimentalOver200K` path only (today that field is xAI-shaped — the name literally encodes xAI's 200k); the durable fix is carrying the side on the tier, e.g. `tier: { type: "context", size: 200_000, inclusive: true }`, so each catalog row maps onto a sentence someone can re-check instead of onto a `199_999` that a later cleanup will round back up.

This cuts both ways, which is why it's worth encoding rather than picking a house style — the same one-token error exists in the *other* direction elsewhere: Helicone's `getPricingTier` uses `value >= threshold` for the 200k Google models (<https://github.com/Helicone/helicone/issues/5788>) and unsloth's studio pricing uses `>= lc_thresh` for the 272k OpenAI models (<https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth/pull/9527>) — both start the expensive tier one token early, because they assumed the same convention globally in the opposite direction.

Re the review's item 3 above — a mirror case one token below is worth adding, but note `199_999` and `200_000` should now give *different* answers for xAI, so it's `estimate(199_999) === 0.399998` / `estimate(200_000) === 0.8`, not a pair that both sit on the base rate.

Also worth flagging alongside item 2: for xAI the whole-request switch is right, and it's right for OpenAI too — "2x input **and 1.5x output** for the full session", with the *input* length selecting the *output* rate. That's what `costInfo.output` already does here. It is **not** right to assume marginal/graduated math for any of the four above; all four say the whole request re-prices.

I keep the cross-vendor version of that table with each row carrying the sentence it came from, if it's useful while deciding the tier shape: <https://xyzs996.github.io/llm-api-pricing/prices.html#same-number-opposite-answer>. Happy to send the boundary test cases as a follow-up PR if you'd rather keep this one scoped to the confi

@Zaczero — your inference from the data is right, and the cause is one line in the Zen OpenAI helper. It also turns out to be two bugs, not one: the second is a straight double-charge on Zen's billing path that nobody has looked at.

### The line

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/main/packages/console/app/src/routes/zen/util/provider/openai.ts#L47-L61

```ts
normalizeUsage: (usage: Usage) => {
  const inputTokens = usage.input_tokens ?? 0
  const cacheReadTokens = usage.input_tokens_details?.cached_tokens ?? undefined
  const cacheWriteTokens = usage.input_tokens_details?.cache_write_tokens ?? undefined
  return {
    inputTokens: inputTokens - (cacheReadTokens ?? 0),   // <-- writes never subtracted
    ...
    cacheWrite5mTokens: cacheWriteTokens,
```

`cached_tokens` is subtracted; `cache_write_tokens` is not. OpenAI's docs say both are subsets of `input_tokens`, with arithmetic rather than prose — the GPT-5.6 sample in "Measure cache reads and writes":

```
usage.input_tokens = 2600
usage.input_tokens_details.cached_tokens = 2000
usage.input_tokens_details.cache_write_tokens = 400
```

> In this example, 2,000 tokens were read from the cache and 400 additional tokens were written.
> The remaining 200 input tokens were neither read nor written.

2,000 + 400 + 200 = 2,600 (<https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching>, read 2026-08-22). So the disjoint non-cached count is `input_tokens - cached_tokens - cache_write_tokens`, and the helper leaves the writes in.

The local side of this same repo already does it correctly — `session.ts` subtracts both, with a comment saying exactly why:

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/blob/main/packages/opencode/src/session/session.ts#L360-L363

### Bug 1 — the threshold, which is what you measured

`handler.ts:1056` sums `inputTokens + cacheRead + cacheWrite5m + cacheWrite1h`. Substituting: `(input_tokens − cached) + cached + written` = **`input_tokens + written`**. The sum overshoots the real prompt by exactly `cache_write_tokens`, every request.

That's your "differ by 3 on almost every row": when nearly all fresh input gets written to cache, `inputTokens (normalised) = written + neither`, so it sits within `neither` of `cacheWrite5mTokens` — 3 tokens on those rows. And it explains the size of the effect: on a well-cached turn `written ≈ inputTokens`, so the sum runs ~2× the prompt and the 200k gate trips at ~100k of real context, which is the "~100k of actual prompt plus a write duplicate" you described. On OpenAI's own sample the sum gives 3,000 for a 2,600-token prompt.

Fixing the helper makes the sum correct *and* leaves the four buckets genuinely disjoint, which is what `handler.ts` assumes. Anthropic's helper needs no change and must not get one — Anthropic's `input_tokens` genuinely excludes both cache buckets, so summing there is already right. That asymmetry is exactly why the fix belongs in the OpenAI helper rather than in `calculateCost`.

### Bug 2 — the same tokens are billed twice

`handler.ts:1060` and `:1067-1070`:

```ts
const inputCost = modelCost.input * inputTokens * 100
...
return modelCost.cacheWrite5m * cacheWrite5mTokens * 100
```

Because the written tokens are still inside `inputTokens`, they are charged at the **input** rate and again at the **cache-write** rate. OpenAI rules that out in the same guide:

> Tokens written to the cache are billed at 1.25× the uncached input token rate.
> It is not an additional charge on top of another full input-token charge.

On `gpt-5.6-luna` ($0.20/M input) a written token should cost $0.25/M; Zen bills it $0.20 + $0.25 = **$0.45/M, 1.8×**. This is unrelated to the tier and applies to every cached OpenAI request through Zen, including ones nowhere near any threshold — so it's a plausible part of the residual $3.37 vs $3.71 gap in the original report even after the tier is fixed. The one-line helper fix closes both.
